facts.statement: The genus Dolichorhynchops was described by Samuel Wendell Williston in 1902.
facts.quote: authority: Williston, 1902

facts.statement: The species D. herschelensis was described by Tamaki Sato in 2005.
facts.quote: subdivision: *†D. herschelensis Sato, 2005

facts.statement: Dolichorhynchops lived in North America during the Late Cretaceous period.
facts.quote: from the Late Cretaceous of North America

facts.statement: The Greek name of the genus means "long-nosed face".
facts.quote: Its Greek generic name means "long-nosed face".

facts.statement: The holotype of D. osborni was discovered by George Fryer Sternberg as a teenager in the upper Smoky Hill Chalk of Logan County, Kansas, around 1900.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen of Dolichorhynchops osborni, KUVP 1300, was discovered in the upper Smoky Hill Chalk Logan County, Kansas, by George Fryer Sternberg, as a teenager, in around 1900.

facts.statement: The holotype was prepared by H.T. Martin and described by Samuel Wendell Williston in 1902.
facts.quote: KUVP 1300 was prepared and mounted by H.T. Martin under the supervision of Dr. Samuel Wendell Williston, who described and named it in 1902.

facts.statement: The specimen FHSM VP-404 was found by Marion Bonner near Russell Springs in Logan County in the early 1950s.
facts.quote: The specimen of D. osborni on exhibit at the Sternberg, FHSM VP-404 was found by Marion Bonner near Russell Springs in Logan County in the early 1950s.

facts.statement: The species D. herschelensis was discovered in the Bearpaw Formation of Saskatchewan, Canada.
facts.quote: D. herschelensis was described as a new species by Tamaki Sato in 2005.

facts.statement: Dolichorhynchops had a long and thin snout with numerous tooth sockets.
facts.quote: The snout is long and thin, with numerous tooth sockets.

facts.statement: Very few of the thin, sharp teeth of Dolichorhynchops remain in the fossil record.
facts.quote: very few of the thin, sharp teeth remain.

facts.statement: D. herschelensis lived during the late Campanian to early Maastrichtian stages of the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: It was discovered in the Bearpaw Formation of Saskatchewan, Canada, a Late Cretaceous (late Campanian to early Maastrichtian) rock formation.

facts.statement: D. herschelensis is estimated to be about 2.5 to 3 meters in length.
facts.quote: Assuming that only a few vertebrae are missing from the skeleton, the animal is estimated to be about 2.5 - 3 m in length.

facts.statement: A 2008 study classified T. bonneri as the valid species D. bonneri within the genus Dolichorhynchops.
facts.quote: A study in 2008 found that T. bonneri is a valid species of Dolichorhynchops, D. bonneri.

facts.statement: D. tropicensis lived in the early Turonian stage of the early Late Cretaceous, approximately 93.5 to 91 million years ago.
facts.quote: It was collected by the Museum of Northern Arizona from a single locality within the Tropic Shale of Utah, dating to the early Turonian stage of the early Late Cretaceous, about 93.5-91 million years ago.

facts.statement: Dolichorhynchops belongs to the family Polycotylidae.
facts.quote: familia: Polycotylidae

facts.statement: Dolichorhynchops is classified within the subfamily Polycotylinae.
facts.quote: subfamilia: Polycotylinae

facts.statement: The genus name means "eye with long nose" in Greek, possibly because its eyes appear positioned further forward on its long snout.
facts.quote: El nombre del género en griego significa "ojo con nariz larga", quizás debido a que sus ojos parecen dispuestos más adelante sobre su largo hocico.

facts.statement: The holotype of Dolichorhynchops osborni was discovered in the Smoky Hill Chalk of Logan County, Kansas, by the teenage George F. Sternberg around the year 1900.
facts.quote: El espécimen holotipo de Dolichorhynchops osborni fue descubierto en Smoky Hill Chalk en Logan County, Kansas, por George F. Sternberg, cando era adolescente, por el año 1900.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen KUVP 1300 was prepared and reconstructed by M.T. Martin under the supervision of Dr. Samuel Wendell Williston, who described and named it in 1902.
facts.quote: KUVP 1300 fue preparado y reconstruido por M.T. Martin bajo la supervisión del Dr. Samuel Wendell Williston, quien los describió y nombró en 1902.

facts.statement: In 1918, Charles H. Sternberg found a large mosasaur, Tylosaurus, containing the remains of a plesiosaur in its stomach.
facts.quote: En 1918, Charles H. Sternberg halló a un gran mosasaurio, Tylosaurus, con restos de un plesiosaurio en su estómago.

facts.statement: George Sternberg found a second, less complete specimen of D. osborni in 1926.
facts.quote: George Sternberg halló a un segundo espécimen menos completo de D.osborni en 1926.

facts.statement: The specimen of D. osborni currently on display at the Sternberg Museum, FHSM VP-404, was found by Marion Bonner near Russell Springs in Logan County in the early 1950s.
facts.quote: El ejemplar de D. osborni en exhibición en el Museo Sternberg, FHSM VP-404 fue hallado por Marion Bonner cerca de Russell Springs en el condado Logan a principios de la década de 1950.

facts.statement: This specimen is perhaps the most complete known of this species and measures just under 3 meters in length.
facts.quote: Este es, quizás, el más completo espécimen conocido de esta especie, y mide algo menos de 3 metros de largo.

facts.statement: Remains from the lower zone of the chalk, dating from the Coniacian to Santonian ages, were reported.
facts.quote: reportó los primeros restos de la zona inferior de la caliza (de edad de entre el Coniaciano al Santoniano).

facts.statement: In 2005, the remains of the oldest known D. osborni were discovered in the Fort Hays Chalk in Jewell County, Kansas.
facts.quote: En 2005, los restos del más antiguo D. osborni conocido fueron descubiertos en la Caliza Fort Hays en el condado de Jewell, Kansas.

facts.statement: D. herschelensis was described as a new species by Tamaki Sato in 2005.
facts.quote: D. herschelensis fue descrito como una especie nueva por Tamaki Sato en 2005.

facts.statement: It was discovered in the Bearpaw Formation of Saskatchewan, Canada, a geological formation from the Late Cretaceous (late Campanian to Maastrichtian).
facts.quote: Fue descubierto en la Formación Bearpaw de Saskatchewan, Canadá, una formación geológica del Cretácico Superior (finales del Campaniense al Maastrichtiense).

facts.statement: The skull, lower jaw, ribs, pelvis, and shoulder blades were collected, but the spine was incomplete, so the exact number of vertebrae in the living animal is unknown.
facts.quote: El cráneo, la mandíbula inferior, costillas, pelvis y omóplatos fueron recolectados, pero la columna vertebral estaba incompleta, entonces el número exacto de vértebras del animal vivo es desconocido.

facts.statement: Assuming only a few vertebrae are missing from the skeleton, the animal is estimated to have measured between 2.5 and 3 meters in length.
facts.quote: Asumiendo que solo unas pocas vértebras hayan desaparecido del esqueleto, se estima que el animal medía entre 2.5 a 3 metros de largo.

facts.statement: The snout is long and slender, with numerous alveoli.
facts.quote: El hocico es largo y delgado, con numerosos alvéolos.

facts.statement: However, very few of the thin, sharp teeth have been found.
facts.quote: Sin embargo, muy pocos de los dientes delgados y afilados han sido hallados.

facts.statement: The parent group of Dolichorhynchops is Dolichorhynchia.
facts.quote: Parent group: Dolichorhynchia

facts.statement: Dolichorhynchops is classified as a reptile.
facts.quote: Class: Reptilia

facts.statement: The time range for Dolichorhynchops is from the Turonian to the Maastrichtian, between 93.9 and 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Turonian to Maastrichtian (93.9 to 66 million years ago)

facts.statement: The holotype specimen has been on display at the University of Kansas Natural History Museum since then.
facts.quote: El espécimen ha estado en exhibición en el Museo de Historia Natural de la U. de Kansas desde entonces.
